To swindle someone means to cheat or trick them — usually to take their money or something valuable — by using lies, false promises, or clever deception.

The person being swindled hands over their money or valuables willingly, but only because they have been fooled. That is what makes swindling different from plain robbery. A robber takes things by force. A swindler takes things by making you trust them.

A pickpocket steals your wallet without you knowing. A swindler makes you hand your wallet over yourself — because you believed their lie.
The Three Things That Always Happen in a Swindle

Whenever someone is swindled, three things are always present:

  1. A lie or trick — The swindler creates a false story, a fake opportunity, or a false identity to gain your trust.
  2. Your willing action — Because you believed the lie, you hand over the money or valuables yourself.
  3. The swindler's gain — They walk away with what you gave them, and you are left with nothing — or worse, with something worthless.
How It Is Used in a Sentence

The most common pattern is:

swindle + [person] + out of + [money/valuables]

This means the person was tricked and lost something as a result.

  • He swindled the old woman out of her life savings.
  • She was swindled out of $10,000 by a fake charity.

You can also use it more simply:

  • The salesman swindled him. (We understand the victim lost something.)
  • Thousands of people were swindled by that company.

And you can use it with "into" when someone was tricked into doing something:

swindle + [person] + into + [doing something]

  • They swindled him into signing over his property.
  • She was swindled into investing in a fake business.

Swindle carries a strong sense of cunning and cold calculation. A swindler is not someone who made a mistake or acted in anger. They planned to deceive you. They studied you, built your trust, told a convincing story, and then took what they wanted. There is a sense of deliberate, clever cruelty in the word.

It also carries a sense of betrayal — because swindling requires the victim to trust the swindler first. You cannot swindle a stranger on the street with no interaction. You have to make them believe you, and then betray that belief.
What Makes Something a Swindle and Not Just a Lie?

A lie by itself is not a swindle. A swindle is a lie with a purpose and a victim who loses something real as a result. If someone lies to make themselves look impressive at a party, that is just a lie. But if someone lies to get you to give them money, property, or something valuable — that is a swindle.
Words Close in Meaning (and How They Differ)

Understanding nearby words will sharpen your understanding of swindle itself.

  • Cheat — A broader word. You can cheat in a game, cheat on a test, or cheat a person. Swindle is more specifically about tricking someone out of money or valuables.
  • Con — Very similar to swindle, but more informal and casual in tone. "Con" is the street-level word; "swindle" sounds slightly more serious and deliberate.
  • Defraud — Means essentially the same thing as swindle, but is a formal, legal term. A judge would say "defraud"; an ordinary person would say "swindle."
  • Scam — Very informal. Similar meaning, but "scam" often refers to the scheme itself (e.g., "It was a scam"), while "swindle" works well as the action being done to a person.
  • Trick — Milder than swindle. You can trick someone harmlessly (like a joke). Swindle always involves real loss for the victim.
Everyday Contexts Where You Will See This Word

• Financial fraud: "Investors were swindled out of millions by the fake hedge fund."
  • Online scams: "He was swindled by someone pretending to sell concert tickets."
  • Identity fraud: "She swindled elderly victims by pretending to be a government official."
  • Informal, lighter use: "I feel like that restaurant swindled me — the portion was tiny for that price!" (Here it is used playfully/hyperbolically, not in a serious legal sense.)

To swindle is to deliberately deceive someone — using lies, tricks, or false promises — so that they hand over their money or something valuable, leaving them with a loss they would never have accepted if they had known the truth.
